Understanding visual metaphors is crucial for computers to grasp complex semantic relationships across different domains. Metaphors convey abstract concepts through explicit comparisons, making them a valuable tool for machines to analyze. However, accurately deciphering the semantic connections within metaphors is a challenging task, especially for machines. To overcome this hurdle, we developed a novel framework that incorporates a two-stage approach: identifying and mapping semantic connections. Our framework, based on a graph-based method, effectively isolates metaphoric expressions from non-metaphoric text and captures the underlying semantic connections. We evaluated our approach on a dataset of visual metaphors, demonstrating its superiority over a context-based baseline method in both tasks. Notably, our approach achieved a high average accuracy of 0.83 in identifying metaphoric expressions and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.75 in semantic mapping tasks. We introduce EarthNets, a comprehensive platform for deep learning-based analysis of remote sensing data. By offering a range of tools and algorithms, EarthNets facilitates hands-on learning through real data application, enabling the assessment of different deep learning techniques. The platform's integrated workflow allows users to import various remote sensing data formats, process and pre-clean data, and experiment with multiple deep learning approaches. A built-in model repository enables the saving and sharing of developed models, while our dynamic stack architecture facilitates new feature addition and updates to EarthNets. We demonstrate the platform's capabilities through several hands-on examples, showcasing its potential in remote sensing data analysis. These demonstrations cover data preprocessing methods, deep learning model development, and the application of EarthNets' model sharing features in multiple deep learning tasks. Our platform is publicly available at https://earthnets.github.io. By providing hands-on learning experiences with real remote sensing data, EarthNets empowers users to explore, experiment with, and evaluate different deep learning-based analysis methods. This enables users to identify the most suitable deep learning approach for their specific remote sensing data analysis tasks. Our platform's integrated model sharing feature further facilitates data-driven decision-making through model evaluation and comparison. We believe EarthNets will serve as a valuable resource for remote sensing professionals, researchers, and students seeking to harness the power of deep learning in remote sensing data analysis. By enabling the development of robust, reliable, and accurate deep learning-based analysis models, EarthNets facilitates data-driven decision-making in various remote sensing applications. These applications range from land cover classification and crop type mapping to urban change detection and the prediction of environmental variables. By providing a comprehensive platform for hands-on learning, EarthNets facilitates the development of robust, reliable, and accurate deep learning-based analysis models, enabling data-driven decision-making in various remote sensing applications. Notably, our results include Hadamard matrices of orders 13 and 27 with corresponding designs of size 26 and 54. In medical image segmentation, the goal is often to provide multiple expert-verified
segmentation interpretations for a single 3D scan. Current evaluation methods measure
segmentation accuracy on individual scans but fall short in addressing the need for
multiple segmentations. This study investigates various strategies to assess the
multiple segmentation predictions generated by a single model. We propose a
framework that combines two standard metrics, the Dice score and the Hausdorff distance,
to effectively evaluate each predicted segmentation in relation to its corresponding
ground-truth scan. We also introduce a new metric, the Conditional Hausdorff Distance,
which assesses the similarity between predicted and true segmentations in terms of
label consistency. Experimental results demonstrate the utility of our framework and
its component metrics in evaluating the performance of segmentation models on 3D
prostate scans. We believe that our framework offers a more comprehensive evaluation
of segmentation models capable of predicting multiple segmentations per scan. The
code implementing our framework is available at https://github.com/NeuroBIOtech/CME.

We present a unified framework for composable Private Information Retrieval (PIR), encompassing various existing forms, thereby streamlining the analysis of its various variants. This framework is based on a novel definition of composable PIR, which synthesizes concepts from prior research, notably that by Chandrasekaran et al. Our framework is versatile, allowing it to accommodate different PIR models, such as those with or without a trusted third party, and in local or distributed server settings. Additionally, it supports a one-time or adaptive access model and different computational models, including a post-quantum variant. By leveraging this framework, we establish optimal security bounds for multiple PIR protocols, including post-quantum PIR and adaptive access PIR, under the standard security definition. Our work also offers a straightforward method for constructing secure composable PIR from garbled interactive proofs. As a result, we establish an optimal security bound for interactive PIR under the standard security definition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our composability framework facilitates the analysis of PIR in more complex scenarios, such as multi-party computations that utilize PIR. Specifically, we show that our framework enables the secure composition of interactive PIR with local interactive commitment over a ring. This is achieved by utilizing the composable PIR framework in conjunction with a locally committed interactive commitment. Our work has potential applications in modeling the security of PIR in more complex scenarios and we plan to explore this in future research. The implementation of our composability framework is accompanied by a practical application in the form of a Post-Quantum PIR implementation. This implementation is based on a new interactive commitment scheme based on a ring where the commitment is local, and it can be used to achieve the optimal security bound for a 2-server 1-dealer setting with adaptive access in $\mathcal{O}(2^{\kappa}\cdot 2^{\kappa} \cdot 2^{\kappa} \cdot Q) 2^{\kappa}$ bits'. We investigate the impact of new physics on electroweak observables, specifically mass, mixing angle, and coupling constant measurements, utilizing a generalized two-Higgs-doublet model. Our analysis reveals that the experimental data on these observables can be reconciled with theoretical predictions made at the Z-pole under two conditions: one, by introducing non-zero Wilson coefficients, and two, by assuming the presence of new physics without significantly increasing the universe's energy density. We also examine the constraints imposed by these conditions and discuss potential future research directions. Furthermore, we present a conceptual design for a future experiment, the P-50 project, which aims to probe within and beyond the Standard Model through precise measurements of the W-boson mass, the forward-backward asymmetry, and the top-quark mass. This proposed experiment would have the capability to explore new beyond-Standard Model physics scenarios, including the presence of new light particles and gauge bosons, and would also enable the discovery of new physics signals at the TeV scale. To this end, we discuss the potential for the P-50 to detect a variety of signals, including the production of new scalar particles, vector-like quarks, and leptons, and to make significant contributions to the Standard Model's anomalous magnetic moments, through the use of a muon storage ring. This would include the measurement of the anomalous magnetic moments of the muon and electron, and the detection of the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. Additionally, we highlight the potential for the P-50 to make significant advancements in our understanding of the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry by studying the production of top-quark pairs. Our analysis also includes a discussion of the challenges associated with implementing a muon storage ring, including the use of muons in the P-50, and the technical difficulties involved in achieving the desired level of precision. These challenges are addressed in detail in our discussion of the P-50's feasibility. To facilitate further research, we provide a set of publicly available Mathematica packages for the analysis of the data from the P-50. These packages can be accessed at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/PhysMaths/P-50. This paper presents a novel method for resolving long-term drift in odometry through loop closure detection using a deep learning-based approach. The proposed system employs a fully convolutional neural network to create a binary similarity map, ranking loop closures based on a pre-trained feature database. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on Gazebo simulations and real-world data collection. The results show that our system achieves up to 100% loop closure accuracy in pre-processed images, a 90% reduction in visual SLAM computation time compared to baseline methods, and 80% less time spent on global localization. The implementation details and quantitative evaluation of our system are made publicly accessible. We introduce SC-Ques, a novel, large-scale question answering dataset consisting of 100,000 sentence completion challenges sourced from a prominent German language dataset (DeReKo). Each associated question effectively gauges the dataset's coverage of the text's content, mirroring real-world scenarios. Additionally, we outline a straightforward abstractive sentence completion model that achieves promising results when validated against the dataset's answers. Notably, this model outperforms the baseline model by 2.6 and 1.5 BLEU-score in the test set. Moreover, we demonstrate that the proposed model excels at answering sentence completion questions without external knowledge on the RoBERTa model. The SC-Ques dataset is now publicly available. For more information and the dataset, visit our website at https://github.com/rohan-karki/sc-ques. We also present a companion report in German: Kritik, Kompromisse und Vorschläge: Eine qualitativ analysierende Untersuchung der Sentence Completion Questions.

By combining a classifier with a model that generates adversarial examples, LADDER can effectively train DNNs to withstand various attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art adversarial training techniques by a margin of 10-30% in different settings. Moreover, under AutoAttack, LADDER outperforms even the best pre-trained models by a margin of 6-9%. Additionally, our method exhibits exceptional generalization capabilities across various datasets and models, achieving remarkable robustness gains. Furthermore, LADDER can be seamlessly integrated with other adversarial training techniques to further enhance model robustness. In particular, we show that combining LADDER with EAD training can achieve superior performance, even outshining the latest advancements in adversarial training. This paper addresses the multi-view detection issue, focusing on distinguishing between various object types within images captured from different angles. Existing research on multi-view detection has primarily centered on separating object types and views, but this approach is limited in its ability to effectively combine features across all views. To address these shortcomings, we propose a new multi-view detection model called the Multi-view Detection with Oriented Feature Fusion (MDFOF) network. This model incorporates an oriented feature encoding mechanism that captures the spatial relationships between features across all views, allowing it to effectively combine oriented features into a unified representation. This unified representation is then used to identify object categories. In addition to this core component, our model includes a spatial attention mechanism that enables dynamic integration of spatial information across all views, as well as a self-attention mechanism that facilitates the exchange of information between different views. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach over current state-of-the-art methods in multi-view detection. Our research investigates the relationship between data representation quality and the performance of state-of-the-art vision transformers on downstream tasks. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between our proposed metric and the performance of downstream classification and object detection tasks, demonstrating that better representation quality leads to improved downstream performance. Additionally, we utilize our representation quality metric to evaluate the impact of data augmentation on representation quality and model robustness, revealing that standard data augmentation methods can degrade representation quality and lead to increased error rates. Our research findings suggest that our proposed representation quality metric can effectively predict the robustness of models and the success of downstream tasks, making it a valuable tool for evaluating neural networks and guiding model development. Cache side channels are a prevalent issue, occurring in at least 30% of major web software, yet detecting them is difficult due to their often-obscure nature in source code.  To address this challenge, CacheOutlook uses a combination of hyperparameter-free statistical models and behavioral analysis to track cache behavior, thereby identifying and quantifying suspicious code segments in software.  Our experiments on real-world web applications demonstrate that CacheOutlook can identify and rank potential vulnerable code segments, with a high success rate in detecting and characterizing known vulnerabilities, and a low false positive rate.  Notably, CacheOutkoit is the first system to provide automated vulnerability ranking capabilities for cache side channels.  Our study is the first to analyze the prevalence of cache side channels in modern web software, with notable cases of cache side channel vulnerabilities affecting prominent web software. This paper introduces a unified framework for evaluating the stability of multi-agent systems, encompassing both consensus and network coalescence. Our concept of stability is grounded in the Lyapunov stability theory and allows various stability measures to be easily applied to multi-agent systems, streamlining the process of selecting appropriate Lyapunov functions for specific multi-agent system analyses. The proposed theory is further demonstrated through its application to multi-agent systems with general linear dynamics and nonlinear network connectivity. The effectiveness of the framework is then validated through the analysis of consensus stability and network convergence in multi-agent systems, accompanied by numerical examples that illustrate its practical application. Ultimately, the proposed unified framework provides a systematic approach to stability analysis in multi-agent systems, enhancing our understanding of these complex systems and facilitating the development of Lyapunov-based stability results for diverse multi-agent system applications. This paper is a comprehensive revision of the earlier work "Consensus Stability in Multi-Agent Systems" published in 2018. The revised paper incorporates significant updates, including the expansion of Lyapunov functions, the addition of new examples, and the integration of supplementary material. These changes substantially enhance the scope and comprehensiveness of the original work, making the revised paper a more valuable contribution to the field. The complete revision is provided in the supplementary material.

In the field of graph representation learning, it's often assumed that a single global representation can effectively capture a graph's topological structure. However, real-world graphs rarely exist in isolation and are often influenced by external factors. This paper posits that a graph's local environment plays a crucial role in shaping its topological structure and, therefore, its embedding. To validate this hypothesis, we propose a novel framework that generates multiple embeddings tailored to specific subgraphs within a graph. The quality of these embeddings is influenced by the density of the subgraph and the density of the surrounding graphs. To mitigate the impact of dense neighborhoods, we employ a novel aggregation method that leverages the similarities between local and global topological structures. The results of our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields more accurate embeddings for nodes in dense graphs, thereby improving downstream tasks such as node classification and clustering. To validate the effectiveness of our framework, we conducted comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets and compared it to state-of-the-art graph embedding algorithms. The application of deep survival models in healthcare has been expanding rapidly, thanks to their superior performance compared to traditional methods. However, the lack of interpretability in deep survival models hinders their adoption in real-world settings. To address this issue, we introduce a novel interpretability technique called reverse survival model (RSM) that generates features explaining model predictions. RSM is a straightforward approach that leverages model predictions to estimate underlying features, then uses observed features to validate model predictions. When applied to two leading deep survival models, DeepHit and PHELS, RSM produced explainable features that matched observed values, making them suitable for clinical applications. RSM's effectiveness was demonstrated through its ability to enhance prediction accuracy and provide more accurate uncertainty estimates for individual subjects. RSM's simplicity and effectiveness make it a valuable tool for clinicians to understand and improve upon the explanations offered by deep survival models. In conventional C-RAN systems with limited fronthaul capacity, backhaul links act as bottlenecks, severely limiting performance. To overcome this, a new C-RAN architecture is proposed, integrating edge computing with RISC-NUMA processors to enhance data processing and communication efficiency. This system utilizes RISC-NUMA processors to split the workload of baseband units, allocating processing duties to general-purpose CPUs and sharing data with specialized accelerators through the fronthaul. As the data volume increases, data is divided among parallel accelerators, enabling concurrent processing and data transmission within the fronthaul. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach significantly minimizes end-to-end latency in comparison to traditional methods, thereby showcasing the potential of RISC-NUMA edge computing in mitigating backhaul bottlenecks. Furthermore, the proposed architecture's low power consumption and high processing speeds make it an attractive solution for future wireless networks. To facilitate the development of RISC-NUMA edge computing systems, a corresponding open-source simulator is made available. Additionally, the authors provide a detailed analysis of the system's design, discussing the key trade-offs between processing duties, data transmission, and parallel accelerators. Ultimately, the authors outline the challenges and potential research avenues for edge computing in future wireless networks. Deep neural network-based reduced-order models (ROMs) are increasingly being used to accelerate the simulation of complex additive manufacturing processes. These models, which learn from high-dimensional input data, have shown great potential in mitigating the computational demands of such processes. Deep neural network-based ROMs are more computationally efficient but less accurate, while k-nearest neighbor ROMs provide more accurate predictions but require more computational resources. These results suggest that the choice of ROM depends on the specific application and highlight the importance of understanding their strengths and limitations. We introduce a novel noise-robust feature extraction method, the learned dynamic filter, which is integrated with a deep neural network. This approach trains a dynamic filter capable of eliminating non-spectral noise in each Time-Frequency chunk within feature maps. Our proposed method enhances the learning process through the application of two key strategies: dividing Time-Frequency features into non-overlapping blocks to prevent interference, and introducing an auxiliary loss to the dynamic filter for more stable training. Our results indicate a significant improvement of up to 10% compared to the existing dynamic filter model in various speech recognition tasks. To address the challenges of a rapidly changing energy system, researchers have developed various capacity expansion models. These models rely on historical data to simulate future energy markets. However, this study reveals that using only past patterns may not accurately predict energy system dynamics. We propose a new method to select a suitable representative period, enhancing the model's accuracy. This study applies the approach to a European energy network simulation and introduces a novel metric to evaluate the model's effectiveness. We discovered that our method significantly outperforms traditional approaches, particularly when it comes to low-carbon scenarios. Furthermore, we found that a more representative period can mitigate the impact of data biases on the model's results. Lastly, we provide guidance on selecting suitable data and periods for capacity expansion modeling purposes. We also propose future research directions to refine this approach. This research introduces an innovative joint learning framework that integrates anonymization and re-identification tasks for pedestrian images. By training anonymization and re-identification models simultaneously, the framework enhances re-identification performance while preserving pedestrian privacy. To achieve this, the framework first learns a person detection model, which is then used to anonymize pedestrian images by redacting sensitive areas. Next, the framework trains a pedestrian re-identification model, which not only improves with anonymized images but also retains anonymized data to prevent overfitting. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, outperforming existing methods in both anonymization and re-identification tasks. Furthermore, the framework's ability to maintain privacy is ensured by redacting sensitive areas and its robustness is demonstrated by its ability to perform well under real-world conditions, such as varying image sizes and shapes. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to explore the joint learning framework in the context of pedestrian image anonymization and re-identification. We introduce the DDF inspector-executor framework, which enhances distributed numerical linear algebra computations on high-performance computing clusters. The framework's inspector-executor approach streamlines sparse matrix multiplication and solves sparse systems of equations by breaking the problem into smaller, localized tasks that are independent of the solver's algorithm. The framework's flexibility and portability make it suitable for various programming languages and high-performance computing libraries. We demonstrate the framework's capabilities in the Petascale Linear Algebra Solvers (PLAS) package and showcase its application in the Exascale Linear Algebra Testing Project (ExaLINPACK). In the realm of online scheduling on multiprocessary systems, we investigate the minimization of makespan in scenarios where tasks are revealed gradually. Our focus is on finding the best way to process tasks in a sequence of time slots, where each slot can accommodate multiple tasks. We consider two types of tasks: those with a fixed duration and those with an unpredictable duration. For tasks with fixed durations, we explore two subcases, one in which tasks can be split across slots and the other where tasks must be contained entirely within a single slot. For tasks with unpredictable durations, we examine a scenario in which tasks can be split across multiple slots. We establish competitive ratios for each scenario and demonstrate that these ratios are optimal, given the constraints of the problem. We also show that a modified First-Come-First-Served algorithm can achieve these ratios. For tasks with predictable durations, we establish that a modified First-Come-Fixed-Duration algorithm can achieve near-optimal makespans. We further investigate the problem of minimizing the makespan under a constraint on the maximum memory used by a single slot and show that a modified First-Come-Fixed-Duration algorithm can achieve near-optimal makespans in this case. Our results are validated through experiments. A novel competitive algorithm is also presented for tasks with unpredictable durations that achieves a competitive ratio of $1 + \frac{1}{k(1 - \epsilon)}$, where $k$ is the number of available processors and $\epsilon$ is a small positive value. This algorithm is notable for not requiring the use of a parameter threshold and for being the first known algorithm to achieve a competitive ratio of $1 + \frac{1}{k}$ for tasks with unpredictable durations. We also demonstrate that a modified version of this algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio of $1 + \frac{1}{k(1 - \epsilon)}$ for the problem of minimizing the maximum memory used by a single slot. Our results are validated through experiments. All of our algorithms and their analyses have been formally verified using the Coq proof assistant. Wasserstein distance offers a geometrically informed approach to measuring divergence between distributions. This study investigates the performance of the Wasserstein $k$-means clustering algorithm in comparison to established clustering methods. It commences by establishing a recovery guarantee for the Wasserstein $k$-means algorithm when data points are drawn independently and identically from a fixed distribution under conditions of $k\leq 2$. Furthermore, an efficient algorithm for solving Wasserstein $k$-means is provided with computational complexity $O(kn\log^2n)$, where $n$ represents the data dimension. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation on both artificially constructed and real-world datasets, the advantages of the Wasserstein $k$-means algorithm are highlighted. Notably, the algorithm exhibits superior performance in handling diverse data types, including images, text, and genomic sequences, in comparison to traditional clustering methods. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the Wasserstein $k$-means algorithm is more resilient to outliers than $k$-means. Our results underscore the potential of the Wasserstein $k$-means algorithm in delivering robust and effective clustering solutions across diverse application domains. Finally, the study explores the application of the Wasserstein $k$-means algorithm in clustering genomic sequences and demonstrates its ability to accurately recover ancestral sequences. In memory-based multi-agent simulation environments, where scalability is a major concern, agent persistence is typically achieved through a centralized approach. However, this method is limited in its ability to scale, as it relies on a single point of failure within the system. In an effort to address this issue, we've developed a new framework for persistent multi-agent simulation that leverages distributed agent persistence. This innovative solution allows for the efficient and scalable management of multi-agent simulations across multiple machines. By utilizing a distributed data storage mechanism that allows agents to persist across machine boundaries, our framework enables the creation of complex agent simulations that cannot be achieved with traditional memory-based environments. Additionally, our framework provides a high level of scalability, allowing it to efficiently handle the creation, management, and destruction of large numbers of agents. In a comparative study, our framework was shown to significantly outperform a popular multi-agent simulation environment, the Swarm Simulator, in terms of creation and destruction time, particularly as the size of the simulation increases. For example, our framework was able to create and destroy 100,000 agents in under 1 second on a 64 core machine, while the Swarm Simulator required over 2 minutes to perform the same task. In contrast, our framework was able to handle 1 million agents in under 2 minutes, while the Swarm Simulator would have taken over 3 days to perform the same task. These results demonstrate the high level of efficiency and scalability that our framework provides for complex multi-agent simulations. Finally, our framework is open source and available for download, providing researchers with a powerful tool for creating scalable, multi-agent simulations. This research investigates the effectiveness of using grammar-based tree-to-tree models for translating programming languages. A new approach is proposed, allowing for the extraction of rules from the source language's abstract syntax tree. These rules are then utilized to construct the target language's AST. Experiments were conducted using the Py2Tree dataset, comparing the performance of the grammar-based model to existing state-of-the-art benchmarks. Results demonstrate that the grammar-based model can match or surpass the state-of-the-art model, achieving notable improvements in translation accuracy on Python to Java and Ruby to Java translation tasks. Notably, the grammar-based model achieves a significant 8.9% and 5.7% increase in exact match accuracy on Python to Java and Ruby to Java translation tasks respectively. Moreover, the model's ability to learn rules enables it to successfully translate unseen code that was previously outside its training data's distribution. A detailed analysis of the learned rules is presented, highlighting their applicability to programming language translation. These results indicate that grammar-based models can effectively translate programming languages and may even surpass existing state-of-the-art benchmarks. This study introduces an adjustable structure for Mel-Frequency Chirp Spectrograms (MFCCs) in the task of speaker verification, which is a key component in speaker recognition systems. The proposed learnable MFCCs are trained end-to-end with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to optimize the entire system. In speaker verification, MFCCs are typically extracted from audio signals using a pre-defined algorithm. However, we found that using a fixed algorithm to extract MFCCs leads to sub-optimal performance. In contrast, our learnable MFCCs improve the equal error rate (EER) from 0.83 to 0.73 on the iVector kit and from 0.95 to 0.89 on the VoxCeleb1 test set. Additionally, our learnable MFCCs outperform static MFCCs on both datasets when used as input for iVector feature learning, reducing EER from 9.53 to 7.89% and from 14.15 to 9.28% respectively. The results confirm that our learnable architecture enables the optimization of MFCCs in a way that significantly improves speaker recognition systems. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of applications, including speech recognition and audio tagging, where MFCCs are commonly used. This research introduces a compact and efficient haze removal framework, consisting of a lightweight prediction module and an enhanced dehazing module. Additionally, a comprehensive evaluation of the method's robustness to various noise conditions is provided, showcasing its ability to effectively handle real-world noisy images. Furthermore, this research highlights the potential of gradient descent methods in combining the strengths of specialized algorithms and offers a versatile framework for addressing speedrun routing in future studies. This paper introduces novel Tatar and Mongolian fast text datasets, built using GIZ by Nsoftech in collaboration with Tatarstan and Kalmykovo institutions, and tailored to the AdaptTB model. The Tatar and Mongolian datasets diverge from English counterparts, as they were created without parallel corpora, and feature unique sentence lengths and token counts. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of our dataset design, including a performance comparison of the AdaptonTB model when trained on each language variant alone and in combination with English data. The results indicate that the wordpiece model yields better outcomes than unigram for both languages across all training configurations. Notably, combining models provides the best performance boost, with wordpiece-based models achieving notable improvements when trained on Tatar-English and Mongolian-English data. Conversely, using the unigram model with Tatar-English data yields better results than combining datasets with English-only training. The monitoring of diabetic foot ulcers through image-to-image translation techniques has the potential to improve the detection of changes in ulcer healing progress. However, existing methods primarily focus on translating normal images to actual ulcer images, neglecting the reverse translation from real to synthetic images. We propose that detecting the "inverse translation effect" can significantly enhance the detection of changes in ulcer healing progress. To this end, we introduce a new diagnostic tool, the inverse translation detection (ITD) method, that leverages a conditional generative adversarial network to detect this effect. Our experiments demonstrate that combining ITD with image-to-image translation yields a more accurate diagnostic tool, outperforming existing methods in detecting changes in ulcer healing progress. Moreover, ITD can be integrated with various translation models without compromising performance. Our study is the first to explore this novel approach for monitoring diabetic foot ulcers. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, but their computational complexity and power consumption are significant. Pruning and quantization have emerged as effective methods to reduce this impact. This paper introduces a novel approach called PRoF that leverages the pruning and quantization of CNN filters to minimize computational complexity. PRoF first applies pruning to the most critical CNN filter components in a layer and assesses the remaining network performance. It then identifies the least important remaining components and applies quantization to achieve further efficiency. Experimental results on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that PRoF yields superior performance compared to existing pruning and quantization methods. Furthermore, PRoF offers a flexible balance between performance gain and computational speedup across different datasets. The concept of fairness in machine learning algorithms has recently gained significant attention, with researchers seeking to develop methods for assessing fairness.  We introduce a novel framework based on optimal transport theory to evaluate fairness in machine learning classifiers. Our approach is grounded in the idea that classifiers should treat similar individuals equally, which can be formally represented through the metric OT^2_dist. This metric not only captures disparities in predictive probabilities but also quantifies the underlying reasons for such disparities. Our work provides a mathematical justification for our approach and conducts a thorough empirical evaluation, which reveals that it is as effective as more complex methods while requiring less data. Additionally, our method is shown to be robust and efficient in handling algorithms that are difficult to test for fairness. We also show that it is possible to use OT^2_dist to evaluate the overall fairness of a classifier and to identify the underlying reasons for unfairness. As an example application, we use OT^2_dist to evaluate the fairness of a classifier in the context of loan applicants and identify areas where the classifier may be biased. Our approach is also compared to other state-of-the-art methods for assessing fairness. Overall, our work provides a more interpretable and efficient method for assessing classifier fairness. Artificial neural networks have demonstrated exceptional performance in a wide array of tasks, but their vulnerability to noise remains a significant concern. Previous research has primarily focused on the impact of white noise, whereas real-world applications often involve diverse noise types. This paper investigates the effects of various noise types on artificial neural networks, including Gaussian, uniform, and Cauchy noise, as well as sparse and impulse noise. We also explore the impact of noise on both linear and nonlinear regression, revealing that these models are susceptible to different types of noise. Notably, we find that Gaussian noise affects both linear and nonlinear models equally, whereas white, uniform, and sparse noises primarily impact nonlinear models. In contrast, Cauchy noise affects both types of models, as do impulse noise and mixed noise types. Our findings indicate that introducing noise into models can lead to overfitting, which may be mitigated by incorporating noise into the training process. This paper also introduces a novel, two-stage training method that incorporates noise into the training process. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through numerical experiments, which show that it outperforms traditional training methods, particularly in the presence of noise. Our results suggest that this method has the potential to significantly improve the performance of artificial neural networks in noisy environments, offering a valuable contribution to the field of machine learning. This paper also includes a supplementary video that illustrates the experiments described in the study. We plan to release the associated code, data, and video as open-source resources to facilitate further research and applications. In addition, we have developed a user-friendly web application that enables users to experiment with the proposed method in a more interactive environment. This application is designed to be easily accessible to a wide range of users, including those without extensive programming expertise. We hope that our work will stimulate further research in the field of noisy neural networks and contribute to the development of more robust machine learning techniques. Utilizing a wave number cutoff that respects Lorentz invariance, we find that the energy remains constant across all space, regardless of the cutoff parameter. This result is confirmed through multiple wave function interpretations and a wave length-based cutoff that preserves Lorentz invariance. However, when the wave number cutoff is not constrained by spatial homogeneity, negative vacuum energy becomes possible, depending on the orientation of the wave number vector. This finding also reveals an inconsistency in applying wave function cutoffs to determine vacuum energy. On the other hand, the wave length cutoff consistently produces a finite, non-negative energy value. We also discover that the energy value is directly proportional to the cutoff parameter. This observation raises questions about the energy's behavior as the cutoff parameter approaches infinity. We also examine the energy's dependence on spatial homogeneity constraints. Additionally, we investigate the energy's behavior in the presence of a wave number cutoff that is not constrained by spatial homogeneity and find that the energy's sign is determined by the orientation of the wave number vector. This result is further supported by a wave function cutoff that preserves spatial homogeneity. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings on the cosmological constant problem. This method enables the determination of individual layer importance, facilitating a more targeted pruning process. The ability to understand human visual attention is crucial for the development of advanced visual search and recommendation systems.  In this study, we investigated the visual attention patterns of users during photo evaluation tasks, and how these patterns change when users have limited time to inspect the photos.  In our experiment, 35 participants were presented with 36 images and asked to identify specific objects within a short timeframe.  We used eye-tracking technology to record users' gaze data and analyzed it using various metrics, including fixation duration and frequency.  We then compared the results from users who were given different time constraints and discovered that users' attention patterns changed significantly when time was limited, with shorter fixations and fewer fixations overall.  We also found that users who had more time to inspect the photos tended to identify more objects.  Our results have important implications for the design of visual search and recommendation systems, as well as advertising targeting systems, that rely on understanding human visual attention.  We believe that our findings can contribute to the development of more effective and user-friendly systems. Our complex-valued model is effectively applied to a variational autoencoder, resulting in a more efficient RGB representation. Notably, we've observed that, contrary to expectations, the imaginary part often proves to be just as informative as the real part for capturing image content. Our proposed representation can be particularly useful in image generation tasks, where it facilitates the creation of diverse and high-quality images. FlexMatch is a novel semi-supervised learning technique grounded in the FlexCross-Entropy loss function, which unifies the optimization of both labeled and unlabeled data. Unlike traditional methods like FixMatch that rigidly enforce a consistency threshold across all unlabeled data, FlexMatch dynamically adjusts the threshold based on the confidence of individual predictions. This dynamic approach is further enhanced by a user-configurable threshold decay mechanism, which decays the threshold for confident predictions. As a result, FlexMatch is highly adaptable and versatile, seamlessly integrating with existing loss functions like FlexCross-Entropy and a range of consistency losses. In multilingual BERT, fine-tuning occurs at two levels: it refines both the 
multilingual encoder and the language-neutral task predictor. However, we found 
that the predictive task alone is sufficient for training the latter. 
Therefore, we propose a simplified version of multilingual BERT, where the 
predictor is trained independently, leading to a reduction in computational costs 
without a significant performance decline. Additionally, we found that the 
predictor is highly sensitive to the amount of training data available for a 
specific language. To mitigate this issue, we developed a method for adapting the 
predictor using a limited amount of data. Our adaptation technique, which relies on 
self-supervised pre-training, significantly improves the predictor's ability to 
generalize to unseen data. We tested this technique in zero-shot translation 
tasks and achieved substantial improvements over the baseline in 5 languages. 
Our simplified multilingual BERT version and adaptation technique are available 
open-source. We also released a translation dataset with English as the source 
language, which includes 14,000 to 73,000 sentence pairs for each of 11 target 
languages. This resource can be used to train and adapt multilingual language models.

However, these methods often overlook users' and items' inherent characteristics, which are essential for personalized recommendations. Our approach involves utilizing a contrastive loss function to learn unbiased user-item embeddings and an update mechanism to refine these embeddings based on interaction data. By combining these components, we significantly improve recommendation performance on real-world datasets. Accident prediction is a pressing concern for both urban planners and autonomous vehicle developers. Current models for accident forecasting have focused on analyzing traffic data, but often overlook the complex relationships between accidents and various traffic elements. To address this limitation, a novel framework, Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Attention (DSSTA), is presented, which incorporates a spatial-temporal attention mechanism to highlight the most relevant traffic elements at each location and time point. Experimental results on a large-scale traffic accident dataset demonstrate that the proposed DSSTA framework significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving an average improvement in AUC of 4.6%, and in accident frequency prediction, it yields an average improvement of 0.35 events per km^2 per year. Furthermore, the attention mechanism allows for the identification of high-risk traffic areas through attention weights analysis. Moreover, by utilizing attention weights, a novel method for prioritizing accident prevention efforts is introduced, resulting in accident rates declining by 23.6% in areas with focused interventions. As far as known, DialogGPT represents the first AI system to successfully integrate knowledge graphs and long-context question answering in conversational AI. This adaptation process is facilitated through a novel framework that combines two generative models: a pre-existing model for an initial domain and a new model for the target domain. The two models are connected through a latent space, and a technique called selective adversarial domain translation is employed to adapt the target domain model. This technique involves translating samples from the target domain into a latent space, and combining them with samples from the initial domain model. The results show that this approach is effective in adapting to different datasets with minimal additional training, resulting in improved performance on challenging tasks such as unconditional image generation and image translation. Furthermore, this approach is shown to generalize to multiple domains, and the experiments demonstrate its potential in real-world applications. For example, this approach is shown to generate realistic images of people with different ages using a single model, and to produce images of vehicles with varying styles without the need for multiple models. This represents a significant reduction in the cost and time required to develop and train such image generation models. This study investigates the resilience of multilingual language models by introducing a new dataset called Multilingual Natural Adversarial Examples and examines the impact of different language capabilities on model robustness. Interestingly, researchers discovered that multilingual models tend to be more resistant to these manipulations than their monolingual counterparts. To explore the underlying reasons for this, researchers developed and analyzed a range of models, including monolingual, multilingual, and bilingual models, which revealed key insights. The study found that bilingual models, which can process both original and translated text, are more resistant to these manipulations than monolingual models. This led to the identification of a new model architecture called the Cross-lingual Masked Language Model, which combines the benefits of both monolingual and bilingual models. This architecture was found to achieve superior performance in cross-lingual settings and, crucially, remains highly robust under various types of manipulations. This led to the development of a novel model called the Cross-lingual Masked Language Model-based classifier, which outperforms its bilingual counterpart while maintaining comparable robustness. This study's findings provide a deeper understanding of the impact of language capabilities on model robustness and offer a practical approach to developing models that can effectively handle multiple languages while withstanding various types of manipulations. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that focuses on restoring images based on their intrinsic restoration potential. As a result, images with low restoration potential are given higher priority for restoration processing, leading to improved visual quality. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains in image quality, specifically up to 1.6 dB higher PSNR, compared to conventional methods without restoration potential assessment. The proposed technique can be seamlessly integrated into various image enhancement algorithms to maximize their potential. Current Visual Question Answering models struggle with providing reliable answers in real-world applications due to their reliance on specific training data features. These models often fail when presented with novel situations not seen during training, leading to incorrect answers. To overcome this challenge, we focus on developing more adaptable VQAs that can generate accurate answers even in unfamiliar environments. To achieve this goal, we introduce a new task called Unseen Visual Question Answering, where VQAs are required to produce valid answers for questions that don't involve novel situations but do involve unseen objects, as well as questions involving novel situations that include familiar objects. To tackle this task, we propose a two-stage training approach, which first trains the VQA model to generate answers for questions without novel situations and then fine-tunes it to accommodate novel situations involving familiar objects. To evaluate the adaptability of our proposed VQAs, we created a new dataset called Unseen-VQA, which includes 3,500 questions divided into two categories: 1,500 questions without novel situations and 1,900 questions involving novel situations. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed VQAs achieve a 71.1% accuracy on Unseen-VQA without any additional training, while a simple fine-tuning approach boosts the accuracy to 82.1%. We introduce IBIS-CNN, a novel CNN-based approach for estimating heart rate from single images. Unlike previous methods, our approach uses a fully end-to-end trainable model that can be applied to images without requiring RGB data. By incorporating motion cues from the image, IBIS-CNN significantly outperforms existing image-based heart rate estimation methods, achieving a lower error margin of 3.76BPM on the largest public dataset. Moreover, our approach demonstrates improved robustness against image noise and distortion, making it a reliable tool for remote healthcare monitoring. The proposed method is compatible with any CNN model and its pre-trained weights can be reused, thereby facilitating efficient heart rate estimation from images. Recommendation systems in streaming platforms face a unique challenge: users not only expect to discover new content, but also want to be guided in watching it. These systems must navigate the complexities of content consumption and provide users with tailored suggestions for their individual needs. This new quantification technique, known as the cross-sectional area method, calculates the calcium volume of individual coronary arteries by integrating cross-sectional areas of the arteries over time. In contrast to traditional calcium scoring methods that measure the integrated density of calcium from the non-contrast data, this new method provides improved reproducibility. To overcome this, we propose an innovative approach that combines model predictions with user input, allowing users to annotate regions of interest.  By leveraging these user annotations, our method updates the model's weights, significantly improving image segmentation performance.  The updated model provides users with more accurate segmentation suggestions, enabling them to more efficiently label the ground truth.  Through this collaborative process, our method demonstrates substantial performance gains, in some cases doubling the accuracy of the initial model. The insights gained from this research can also inform the design of interactive tools for data labeling and can be applied to other applications requiring active learning. Private machine learning models are increasingly being developed to safeguard sensitive data and protect users, enabling fair data sharing among them.  The privacy of each user's data is protected by ensuring that the model shared among users doesn't reveal their individual information.  The challenge of private prediction arises when users want to train a model on shared data while keeping their own information private.  The current state of private prediction methods is characterized by either differential privacy or statistical privacy.  The former involves introducing noise to the model, while the latter involves conditioning the model on a noise-based perturbation.  The former often results in subpar performance, especially in regression tasks, due to introduced noise.  The latter, however, has been shown to outperform differential privacy methods, but its underlying assumptions are often overly restrictive.  The authors of this study propose a new approach that combines the strengths of both methods, leveraging statistical privacy while relaxing its underlying assumptions.  The authors also propose a new framework for private prediction, called the $\epsilon$-clustered-concentrated risk framework, and develop a new algorithm, called the $\epsilon$-C$^2$HDP, that achieves better results than existing methods in both synthetic and real-world datasets.  The proposed algorithm's theoretical guarantees also ensure that its privacy risk is bounded by a certain threshold.  The authors also demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach in handling large datasets by proposing a new framework for distributed private prediction, called the distributed privacy-preserving gradient descent algorithm, and show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of both efficiency and accuracy.  The proposed framework's theoretical guarantees also ensure that its privacy risk is bounded by a certain threshold.  The authors also provide an implementation of their methods, including the $\epsilon$-C$^2$HDP and the distributed privacy-preserving gradient descent algorithm, in the open-source privacy-preserving machine learning library, called the Pymminv library.  The implementation is available at https://github.com/ashish-batta/pymminv.  The authors also provide an overview of their methods, including the $\epsilon$-C$^2$HDP and the distributed privacy-preserving gradient descent algorithm, in the attached slides. Finally, our framework demonstrates excellent scalability, enabling it to efficiently process code traces containing millions of lines of code. Recent advancements in spoken language understanding (SLU) have been significantly facilitated by the development of large, publicly available datasets. Yet, these datasets often fail to accurately represent real-world scenarios due to their limited size and annotation biases. Consequently, models trained on such datasets frequently struggle to generalize effectively to new data. In an effort to address this challenge, we investigated the impact of incorporating real-world observers on the performance of an SLU model. We developed a novel approach, combining both observer-driven supervision and example-driven training, which leverages human input and manual correction to correct classification errors. Our experiments demonstrate that this combined method yields substantial improvements in generalization accuracy across multiple public datasets. Moreover, we introduce a new human-annotated dataset, WebMedia, which features a diverse range of spoken language understanding tasks, along with the corresponding code and models for public access. Our research suggests that integrating real-world observers with data-driven training methods can yield more robust and generalizable spoken language understanding models. This research examines how the electronic properties of intermetallic silicides change in response to hydrogen absorption. Firstly, it causes electride electrons to hybridize with 3p states of hydrogen, resulting in a range of hybridization strengths across different materials. Secondly, hydrogen atoms can occupy interstitial sites, introducing strong local correlations that affect electronic states. Our study demonstrates that these correlations are most significant in Ti5Si3 and Ti5Si4 when they are in a hydride form, leading to distinct electronic structures. Furthermore, we have identified a metallic ground state in HD-Ti5Si3, attributed to the emergence of a Fermi surface resulting from the formation of electride bands and a 3p-Ti hybrid band. In contrast, our calculations show that HD-Ti5Si2 has a semiconducting ground state, characterized by a small bandgap. Our analysis of the density of states and band structures reveals that this material has a similar electronic arrangement to that of HD-Ti5Si3, despite its different ground state properties. Overall, our research highlights the importance of considering the effects of strong correlations in the study of intermetallic silicides and hydrogen, particularly in the context of band formation and gap creation. These findings have significant implications for understanding the properties of these materials and their potential applications in hydrogen storage. This paper introduces a novel approach, the center-aware depth encoding (CDE) task, to improve depth prediction accuracy. The findings also imply that, under specific conditions, it is possible to completely eliminate the negative effects of noise on the intended user's estimation process without compromising the eavesdroper's benefits. Recent breakthroughs in robust training methods have significantly improved the balance between robustness and accuracy in various robot learning applications. However, these advances have largely been confined to supervised learning and have yet to be applied to more complex forms of learning. This study investigates the potential of incorporating robust training methods into reinforcement learning, particularly in the context of learning to navigate challenging, partially observable environments. Our research has important implications for the development of more resilient reinforcement learning algorithms that can better withstand unexpected and unpredictable real-world scenarios. Human motion capture is a crucial aspect of human-robot interaction research, with various approaches utilizing single modalities such as IMUs or LiDAR to estimate human pose and shape. However, the limitations of these individual modalities are being addressed through novel multi-modal solutions. This study presents a multi-modal VAE framework that combines the strengths of IMUs and LiDAR data for precise long-term human motion tracking. By leveraging IMUs' temporal consistency and LiDAR's spatial awareness, the proposed method can effectively reconstruct human pose and shape from partial or noisy LiDAR data. Experimental results on a publicly available dataset demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing single-modal and multi-modal VAEs, as well as deep learning-based human pose estimation techniques. Furthermore, the proposed method can be applied to real-world scenarios, as evidenced by its successful deployment on an industrial robotic arm, showcasing its practical utility. Initially, the network model is trained on a dataset of synthetic images, mimicking real-world seismic images, and a set of weights is calculated. These weights are then applied to a real seismic image, enhancing its resolution. A Bayesian estimation technique follows, utilizing a prior distribution constructed from the synthetic dataset to estimate multiple parameters, including background noise, signal resolution, and image quality metrics, from the modified seismic image. The proposed approach is validated using a controlled dataset, demonstrating its efficacy in estimating parameters, such as hydrocarbon thickness, and highlighting its practicality by reducing the complexity of interpretation. Furthermore, the study showcases the application of this method to a real-world dataset, revealing its potential to streamline the interpretation process. Notably, the proposed approach can be adapted to interpret various geological attributes, such as faults, and its effectiveness is illustrated by its successful application to a real-world dataset in the North Sea area. Additionally, the study showcases the application of this method to interpret faults, and showcases the results obtained. This research presents a novel approach to adversarial training that can effectively counter black-box attacks in complex vision-based systems. The proposed method, called one-shot generative adversarial training, utilizes a conditional generative adversarial network to simulate samples from previously unseen classes. These samples are then utilized to train a discriminator network, enabling it to accurately classify unseen classes. By leveraging this simulated data, the training process becomes more robust and resilient to black-box attacks. Furthermore, our one-shot method significantly accelerates adversarial training, completing the process in just a single pass through the training data, as opposed to multiple passes employed by existing methods. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach successfully defends against black-box attacks on state-of-the-art models, as well as models specifically designed to be adversarially robust, across various benchmarks. Recent advances in machine learning have led to the development of models capable of capturing complex patterns in time series data, including correlations and structural changes. However, existing piecewise stationary time series models often overlook the potential benefits of incorporating prior domain information. We propose a novel approach, Constrained Piecewise Stationarity, that integrates prior knowledge with a flexible time series model. By combining a prior that splits time series into homogeneous segments with a model that estimates segment-specific parameters, C-PS ensures consistency. We further develop a Monte Carlo method to sample from the resulting posterior distribution and demonstrate its efficacy on both simulated and real-world datasets. The results validate C-PS as an effective tool for identifying patterns in time series data. Additionally, we apply this approach to a real-world case study involving the analysis of historical UK temperature data. The analysis reveals a positive correlation between temperature increase and human activity. By incorporating domain-specific prior information, C-PS provides a more accurate and efficient framework for segmenting time series data, compared to models without such priors. The approach can be extended to accommodate multiple prior domains, enabling a more nuanced understanding of time series patterns.
